title: Macrotasks, Microtasks & The Event Loop Architecture
summary: Master the browser and Node.js event loop: understand the call stack, Web APIs, the microtask queue, macrotask queue, and rendering intervals.
learningObjectives: Predict exact console output ordering across synchronous code, Promise microtasks, and setTimeout macrotasks
Prevent UI freezes and event loop starvation by breaking heavy computational work into non-blocking chunks

sections.heading: 1. The Single-Threaded Event Loop & Queue Priorities
sections.content:
JavaScript is single-threaded: it has one Call Stack and executes one instruction at a time. Concurrency in JavaScript is provided by the Event Loop host environment (browser or Node.js runtime).

When asynchronous operations (network fetch, disk read, timer) are initiated, JavaScript delegates them to background threads (browser C++ Web APIs or Node's libuv thread pool) and continues executing synchronous code on the call stack.

When background tasks complete, their callbacks enter one of two queues:
1. Microtask Queue: Highest priority! Holds `Promise.then/catch/finally` callbacks, `queueMicrotask()`, and `MutationObserver` (or `process.nextTick` in Node). The event loop DRAINS THE ENTIRE microtask queue immediately as soon as the Call Stack becomes empty, before processing any other work.
2. Macrotask (Task) Queue: Lower priority. Holds `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `setImmediate`, and I/O callbacks. The event loop processes exactly ONE macrotask per tick, then immediately checks and drains the microtask queue again before executing UI renders.

Event Loop Cycle:
Call Stack -> Drain ALL Microtasks -> (Render UI if scheduled) -> Take ONE Macrotask -> Repeat.

codeExamples.explanation: Microtasks are always drained completely before the event loop advances to rendering or macrotasks.

keyPoints: JavaScript handles concurrency via the Event Loop, not multi-threaded call stacks.
Microtasks (Promises) always run before the next macrotask (setTimeout).
An infinite chain of microtasks will starve the event loop, freezing browser tabs or Node.js servers.
commonMistakes: Expecting setTimeout(fn, 0) to execute immediately; it waits until the call stack and all pending microtasks are cleared.
Running CPU-intensive loops synchronously on the main thread, locking up UI rendering and user interactions.

sections.heading: 2. Verifying Queue Scheduling and Non-Blocking Chunking
sections.content: When performing heavy data transformations (e.g. processing 100,000 array items), running synchronously freezes the thread. Yielding to the event loop using `queueMicrotask` or `setTimeout` lets the browser render frames and respond to user clicks smoothly.

codeExamples.explanation: Demonstrates that synchronous lines run first, followed by all queued microtasks, and finally macrotasks.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
1. Synchronous Start
2. Synchronous End
3. Microtask 1 (Promise.then)
4. Microtask 2 (queueMicrotask)
5. Macrotask (setTimeout)

keyPoints: Synchronous execution always finishes before the event loop checks queues.
Microtask queue drains completely on every turn.
commonMistakes: Assuming queueMicrotask yields to UI rendering; only macrotasks (or requestAnimationFrame) allow paint cycles.

exercises.title: Predict and Verify Event Loop Task Order
exercises.objective: Analyze a complex snippet containing Promises, setTimeout, and synchronous calls to trace execution.
exercises.description: Given a snippet interweaving new Promise executor callbacks, .then() chains, and setTimeout calls, write an explanation of the exact execution order connecting each step to Call Stack, Microtask Queue, and Macrotask Queue mechanics.
instructions: Remember: Promise executor functions `new Promise((resolve) => {...})` execute synchronously!
Identify all synchronous log statements first.
List all microtasks queued by resolved promises.
List all macrotasks queued by setTimeout.
hints: new Promise executes its callback synchronously, so C prints immediately after A and before E.
Expected order: A -> C -> E -> D -> B.
exercises.submissionRequirements: Complete all checklist items, test assumptions, and document verification rationale.
evaluationCriteria: Addresses the root architectural/technical challenge accurately
Follows defensive industry standards and edge-case validation
exercises.solutionExplanation: 'A' runs, setTimeout queues 'B' in macrotasks, Promise executor runs 'C' synchronously and queues 'D' in microtasks, 'E' runs, microtasks drain ('D'), macrotask runs ('B').

knowledgeChecks.prompt: In what order are the queues processed once the call stack is empty?

options.text: All microtasks in the queue are drained completely before the next macrotask is executed.
Only macrotasks execute; microtasks are dropped unless explicitly awaited.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: The event loop specification mandates draining the entire microtask queue before moving to rendering or the next macrotask.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Why does the callback inside 'new Promise((resolve) => console.log('X'))' execute immediately?

options.text: Because Promise executor functions are called synchronously during object construction.
Because V8 compiles promises to WebAssembly.
Because it is hoisted to the top of the file.
Because console.log bypasses the event loop.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: The function passed to the Promise constructor is executed synchronously during initialization; only .then() and .catch() callbacks are deferred to microtasks.

recap: JavaScript's event loop prioritizes synchronous code first, followed by draining all pending microtasks, and finally executing macrotasks one by one.
